The copy exists to keep the substrate's row buffer out of the codec, but RecordCodec.decode already guarantees that outcome from the other side, because decodeCanonicalJson copies the argument into a local array before parsing and holds only the parsed value afterwards. Two copies where one suffices is not something a test can observe: no identity, length or content comparison against that array is reachable.

Project.decode consumes this array and returns a Project, which loadProject validates against tenant_projects' id, tenant_id and revision columns before returning it. The array's only path runs into decodeCanonicalJson, which reconstructs it as a private Uint8Array, parses that, and compares it against a re-encoding to enforce canonical form — three reads and no store. Since nothing outside the codec ever sees the array again, and nothing inside keeps it, dropping the caller-side copy leaves every observable value unchanged.

Workspace topology is immutable, so this reader only ever decodes and checks: the blob becomes a Workspace, the Workspace is compared against the row's id, tenant_id, project_id and revision, and the Workspace alone is returned. The decode path is RecordCodec.decode into decodeCanonicalJson, which immediately makes its own Uint8Array from the argument and never publishes it. There is consequently no expression anywhere downstream whose value depends on whether the codec was given the substrate's array or a duplicate of it.

Guest trust records carry the evidence a foreign Membership is checked against, but that evidence travels as a decoded GuestTrust, not as bytes: this line's array is consumed by GuestTrust.decode and never referenced again. decodeCanonicalJson, which every RecordCodec decode funnels through, copies the argument into a local array before parsing and retains only the JSON value it produced. The copy removed by the mutant is therefore the second of two, and only the codec's own copy is load-bearing.

The Role reader has the shortest projection check in the class — the decoded Role's name against the row's name column — and the same buffer discipline as the rest. Role.decode passes the array to decodeCanonicalJson, which builds a private Uint8Array from it and keeps no handle on the original once parsing finishes. A Role, never a buffer, is what leaves the method. Whether the codec read the substrate's row array directly or a copy of it is not a distinction any Role, any error, or any subsequent read can express.

Membership blobs are decoded here and checked against six projection columns, including the canonical scope and subject keys the store indexes on. None of those checks touch the blob: they compare strings derived from the decoded Membership. The array itself reaches only Membership.decode and, through it, decodeCanonicalJson, which copies it into a fresh Uint8Array up front and discards the reference. Removing the outer copy leaves the codec reading the substrate's own array, which it treats identically and never retains.

The bootstrap marker is read on every store open and every control transaction, and its blob's single consumer is TenantBootstrapMarker.decode. That codec is a RecordCodec, so the array is handed to decodeCanonicalJson, copied into a local Uint8Array, parsed, and re-encoded for the canonical-form check, after which the argument is unreferenced. The marker returned to callers holds a TenantId, a PrincipalId and a Revision, never bytes. No ledger state and no error depends on which array the codec was given.

This reader is the one place in the file that does compare a blob — equalBytes(anchor.trustAnchor, bytes(row, "trust_anchor")) — but that comparison reads the trust_anchor column, not the record column this copy protects. The record blob goes only to TenantBootstrapAnchorRecord.decode, which reaches decodeCanonicalJson and copies the argument into its own Uint8Array before parsing. The anchor that escapes exposes trustAnchor through a getter that slices on the way out, so the row's arrays never leave this module.

decodeWatermark decodes the record blob and then compares the resulting InvalidationWatermark against seven projection columns, none of which is the blob. InvalidationWatermark.decode is a RecordCodec decode, so decodeCanonicalJson copies the array into a private Uint8Array, parses it and drops the reference. The watermark's own bytes are re-derived by InvalidationWatermark.encode wherever the store needs to compare records, never taken from the row. The copy the mutant removes therefore has no reader on either side.

Owner edges are decoded inside a try that converts any non-AgentCoreError into a retention corruption, and the decoded ContentOwnerEdge is then checked against the row's owner_key, tenant, actor and ref columns. The blob reaches only ContentOwnerEdge.decode and through it decodeCanonicalJson, which copies the argument into its own Uint8Array before parsing and keeps nothing. Unlike the content blob path in this file, no edge byte array is ever handed to a caller, so there is no buffer whose ownership a test could probe.

Transient lease state is decoded here and validated against the lease row's key, tenant, actor, ref, digest and timestamp columns. The array feeds TransientContentLeaseState.decode alone, and RecordCodec.decode reaches decodeCanonicalJson, which immediately rebuilds the argument as a local Uint8Array and retains only the parsed value. The bytes a lease hands back to a caller come from the content_blobs read, which has its own detachment and its own test; this record blob never leaves decodeLease in any form.

stored.bytes is already a private array: package.ts's bytes() accessor returns value.slice(), so the projection row handed to decodeSnapshot never aliases the substrate's buffer. This second copy is consumed by MetadataSnapshot.decode, which as a RecordCodec decode passes it to decodeCanonicalJson and is copied a third time into that function's own Uint8Array. Whichever of the three the codec parses, it parses the same bytes and retains none of them, and the snapshot's projection check afterwards compares only decoded fields.

The release reader shares the snapshot reader's discipline and its redundancy. stored.bytes arrives already detached from the substrate by the file's bytes() accessor, and the array this line produces is passed to PackageRelease.decode and dropped. Because decodeCanonicalJson constructs its own Uint8Array from whatever it is given, the codec is insulated from aliasing regardless. The immutability check in add() compares stored.bytes against the freshly encoded candidate, and that comparison reads the projection field rather than this expression's value.

Package locks are decoded and checked against the lock_digest, snapshot_digest and snapshot_revision columns plus the caller's expected digest. As with the other two decoders in this class the array is doubly detached before it arrives — bytes() sliced it out of the row — and triply so once decodeCanonicalJson copies it again. No PackageLock carries the array, no caller receives it, and no comparison in the class reads the value this expression produces, so its identity cannot be observed.

decodeIssued has just narrowed the record column with an instanceof Uint8Array test and hands it to AuthorityPermit.decode. That codec is a RecordCodec, so the array reaches decodeCanonicalJson, which copies it into a local Uint8Array, parses the copy, and re-encodes for the canonical check without ever storing the argument. What decodeIssued returns is an AuthorityPermit, whose digest() is recomputed from the decoded record rather than read from the row, so the row's array has no reader once decode returns.

This is the outer of two copies on one line, and ByteRange.read makes it redundant: read ends in bytes.slice(this.offset, end), so it returns a freshly allocated array on every call, for the whole range as well as a partial one. The value the mutant returns is therefore already an array no other object references — not the row buffer, not the store, not the caller's earlier result. A caller editing it cannot reach any state a later get would read, which is the property the outer copy was written to provide.

The inner copy detaches the row buffer before ByteRange.read sees it, and read does not need the protection: its body is bytes.slice(this.offset, end), which allocates a new array and never keeps the one it was given. Dropping the inner copy hands read the array sqliteBytes returned from the row, which read copies out of and discards. The outer slice on the same line then copies once more, so the caller receives an array two allocations removed from the substrate either way.

projectBlueprint has two callers and neither can observe the copy. addBlueprint passes candidateBytes, a Blueprint.encode result created two lines earlier and reachable from nowhere else, and the projection's bytes field is bound straight into the INSERT. decodeBlueprint passes recordBytes from copyCodecBytes, which already sliced, and reads only the projection's name, version and digest before discarding it. In the first case the source array is private to the call; in the second the projection's bytes field is never read at all.

The plan projection reaches writePlan on the add path and equalPlanProjection on the read path. equalPlanProjection compares id, blueprintDigest, packageLockDigest, configDigest and generation, and never bytes, so the read path cannot see this value. On the add path the argument is candidateBytes from MaterializationPlan.encode, allocated inside addPlan and referenced by nothing outside it, so binding it directly rather than a copy of it hands the substrate an array no other code could ever modify.

Generation projections are compared with equalGenerationProjection, which reads id, actor kind and id, the three origin digests and the generation counter — every field except bytes. The read path therefore never inspects this expression's result. The write path supplies a MaterializationGeneration.encode output created in the same statement sequence that calls project, so the array has no other holder and the substrate receives bytes nothing else can edit whether or not it is copied first.

Managed-state projections carry the desired digest that decides whether a record needs applying, and equalManagedStateProjection compares that digest along with the id, generation, actor, logical key and record kind — never the bytes field this line fills. Reads therefore discard it. Writes fill it from a freshly encoded candidate whose array is local to the enclosing call, so the copy protects against a mutation no reachable code can perform.

The generation pointer is the record a CAS update swaps, and its projection is compared through equalGenerationPointerProjection on actor kind and id, deployment id, generation id and revision. The bytes field takes no part in that comparison, so a pointer read cannot distinguish a copy from the array it copies. On the write side the projection's bytes come from an encode result held only by the calling frame, which is the same guarantee the copy would have supplied.

Forcing the length test true leaves left.every(...), which iterates left's indices only and so answers true whenever left is a prefix of right, including a strict one. Every argument at all four call sites is a RecordCodec encode result — Grant.encode twice, Binding.encode twice, and the previousBytes/nextBytes pair that are themselves Binding.encode outputs — so both sides are complete canonical JSON documents. A complete JSON text has balanced delimiters and ends at its closing brace, so no such document is a strict prefix of another, and the divergent case cannot be constructed. The complementary shortening, left longer than right, still compares undefined and returns false.

bytesEqual has two callers and both pass InvalidationWatermark.encode results on both sides: the previousBytes/nextBytes no-op check, and the read-back comparison that re-encodes the stored watermark against the one just written. Dropping the length test leaves every(), which walks left's indices and therefore returns true for a left that is a strict prefix of right. Canonical JSON envelopes close at their final brace and carry nothing after it, so one cannot be a proper prefix of another; no watermark pair can reach the case where the two forms disagree.

The three call sites all read equalBytes(stored.bytes, candidateBytes), and each is preceded on the line above by decodeSnapshot, decodeRelease or decodeLock over the same stored.bytes. Those decoders reach decodeCanonicalJson, which refuses anything that is not a complete canonical JSON document — it re-encodes what it parsed and compares. So by the time the comparison runs, both arguments are known-complete envelopes, and a complete JSON text cannot be a strict prefix of another because it ends at its own closing brace. Only that case separates every() from the length-guarded conjunction.

Slot comparisons are encode-against-encode at all four sites: insertSlot and install compare SlotDeclaration.encode outputs, insertEntry and contribute compare SlotEntry.encode outputs. Both operands are therefore whole canonical JSON envelopes. Removing the length test lets every() decide, and every() over left's indices differs from the guarded form only when left is a strict prefix of right — impossible between two complete JSON documents, whose text terminates at the closing brace of the top-level object with nothing following it.

This helper has a single caller, put()'s read-back check, and by the time it runs validateContentRow has already established that the stored row's digest equals Digest.sha256 of the bytes it returned, that the row's ref equals the ref derived from the caller's array, and that ref.digest equals that digest. The two arguments therefore have the same SHA-256. Exhibiting a length difference here means exhibiting a SHA-256 collision, which no test can do, so the length test is true whenever it is evaluated and forcing it true changes nothing.

entries.mutated: left.byteLength === right.byteLength && left.every((value, index) => value === right[index])
entries.proof: The mutant makes equalBytes answer true unconditionally. Its only caller is the clause `content === undefined || !equalBytes(content.bytes, detached)` in put(), and the equalBytes half of that disjunction is already unreachable as a refusal: loadSqliteContent has run validateContentRow, which throws corruptContent unless the row's ref, digest and the SHA-256 of its bytes all agree with the digest taken from the caller's array. Two arrays with equal SHA-256 are equal short of a collision, so the original returns true on every input the call site can produce.

entries.replacement: left.byteLength === right.byteLength || left.every((value, index) => value === right[index])
entries.mutated: left.byteLength === right.byteLength && left.every((value, index) => value === right[index])
entries.proof: Turning the conjunction into a disjunction can only widen the set of pairs reported equal, and at this helper's single call site the original already reports equal every time. put() reaches equalBytes only after validateContentRow accepted the row, and that acceptance requires the stored bytes to hash to the same SHA-256 as the array the caller supplied. Both operands are consequently true, so `&&` and `||` return the same value, and no test can drive the call site to a pair where they part without producing a SHA-256 collision.

Forcing the per-byte comparison true makes every() vacuously true, so equalBytes reduces to its length test. That weakening is invisible at the one call site: put() has already passed validateContentRow, which pins the stored row's digest to the SHA-256 of its own bytes and pins that digest to the one derived from the caller's array, so the two arrays agree byte for byte unless SHA-256 collides. Where the arrays agree, the real predicate is true at every index and the mutant returns the same answer the original does.

The lease acquisition read-back is the only caller. Before it, validateBindingBytes has pinned Digest.sha256 of the caller's array to binding.digest and binding.digest to binding.ref.digest, and loadSqliteContent's validateContentRow has pinned the SHA-256 of the persisted bytes to the digest recorded under that same ref. The two arrays therefore share a SHA-256 and cannot differ in length without a collision. Forcing the length test true leaves every(), which agrees with the original on equal arrays.

entries.mutated: left.byteLength === right.byteLength && left.every((value, index) => value === right[index])
entries.proof: equalBytes answering true unconditionally cannot change the acquisition path, because it already answers true there. The clause it feeds refuses a lease when the content read back differs from the bytes supplied, and both have been tied to binding.digest by then: validateBindingBytes hashes the caller's array against it, and validateContentRow hashes the stored row's bytes against the digest filed under binding.ref, which the binding check pinned to the same value. Distinguishing the mutant needs two arrays with one SHA-256.

entries.replacement: left.byteLength === right.byteLength || left.every((value, index) => value === right[index])
entries.mutated: left.byteLength === right.byteLength && left.every((value, index) => value === right[index])
entries.proof: Both operands of this conjunction are true whenever the helper runs, so replacing `&&` with `||` returns the same value. The single call site compares the content row read back inside the acquisition transaction against the array the caller handed in, and the digest chain — caller array to binding.digest through validateBindingBytes, stored bytes to the row digest through validateContentRow, row digest to binding.ref.digest through the ref the read was keyed on — leaves the two arrays equal unless SHA-256 collides.

With the element comparison forced true, every() is vacuously true and equalBytes becomes its length test alone. The lease acquisition path cannot see the difference: the array read back from content_blobs and the array the caller supplied are both pinned to binding.digest by validateContentRow and validateBindingBytes respectively, so they are byte-identical short of a SHA-256 collision, and on byte-identical arrays the true predicate and the forced one agree at every index.

This operand refuses a lease whose content did not persist as supplied, and it can never fire. Reaching it means bytes was defined, so validateBindingBytes ran and pinned Digest.sha256(bytes) to binding.digest and binding.digest to binding.ref.digest; loadSqliteContent then read content_blobs at binding.ref, and validateContentRow refuses that row unless the SHA-256 of the bytes it returns equals the digest filed under that ref. The two arrays therefore share a digest, equalBytes is true, and the negation is false on every input. The `persisted === undefined` operand beside it keeps deciding.

inactiveBoundary has three callers and none can reach this test with an active lease. The acquisition path only assigns `replaced` in the branch where existing.isActive(operationAt) was false, and passes that same operationAt. The close path passes a lease whose closedAt is defined, which returns from the branch above this one. The sweep passes a lease from the else of if (lease.isActive(observedAt)), with the same observedAt. The test is constantly false, so forcing it false selects the branch it already selects.

This literal is the message of a corruptRetention built only inside the active-lease guard, and that guard's test is constantly false for the reason recorded against it: all three callers either pass a lease with a defined closedAt, which returns earlier, or a lease they have just observed to be inactive at the very instant they pass. The error is never constructed and the string never read, so blanking it changes no value any caller, log or assertion could inspect. That is stronger than the prose tolerance a reachable throw would get.

AuthorityRecordChanges.record consults its presence argument exactly once, as `presence === "replaced"`, and uses it only to populate the #replaced set. That set is read back through replaced() and isCreated(), and for the epochs collection neither is ever called: AuthorityClosure reads this.changed.epochs.written() and nothing else, which the class documents by noting that nothing points at a Scope epoch. Blanking the literal moves the epoch key out of a set no code reads, so no audit, error or stored record can differ.

Presence reaches only one test in the whole codebase, `presence === "replaced"` inside AuthorityRecordChanges.record, and the empty string fails it exactly as "created" does — so the #replaced set is identical either way. The claim does not even need that: workspaces are the one collection whose replaced() is never called, because AuthorityClosure audits this.changed.workspaces.written() alone, and saveWorkspace refuses any Workspace whose id already resolves, so nothing here is ever a replacement to begin with.

Workspace's own constructor throws "Workspace topology requires immutable revision zero" for any other revision, and every Workspace reaches this store through it, including the ones Workspace.decode builds. The operand is therefore constantly false and the Project existence check beside it decides alone. It is written because the refusal names both preconditions, and a reader of the SQLite store would otherwise have to know the record type enforces one of them; the equivalent operand in the memory backing's createWorkspace carries the same reasoning.

recordPresence's result travels to AuthorityRecordChanges.record, whose only use of it is the test `presence === "replaced"`. The empty string fails that test on exactly the inputs "created" fails it on, so the #replaced set, and with it replaced(), isCreated(), and every audit set AuthorityClosure derives from them, are bit-for-bit what they were. No other code reads an AuthorityRecordPresence value, and the changeset never leaves the store: it is private to the active write and passed only to assertCompleteClosure.

Three operands above this one, `marker.revision.value !== Revision.initial().value` throws unless the stored marker's revision is exactly zero, so by the time this comparison is evaluated its right-hand side is zero. Its left-hand side is a Revision's value, and Revision's constructor refuses anything that is not a non-negative safe integer, a constraint every decode path goes through. A non-negative number is never less than zero, so the operand is constantly false and the loadPrincipal check after it decides. Kept rather than deleted so that relaxing the pin above refutes this proof instead of silently reviving dead code.

some and every differ only on an array with mixed results or on the empty array. plan.grants is createTenantControlBootstrapPlan's materialization of OWNER_ROLE over the owner Membership, and builtInRole constructs every built-in with a single RoleRule, so the materializer emits exactly one desired record and the array always holds one Grant. On a one-element array the two quantifiers agree by definition. The sibling call on plan.roles is killed instead, because BUILT_IN_ROLES holds three.

This is the left operand's default, and it is never taken. All three callers pass a TenantBootstrapAnchorRecord as `left`: two compare the anchor loaded from storage against a caller-supplied one, and the third compares the loaded anchor against the record just built. That class declares tenantKind as a required TenantKind and assigns it `anchor.tenantKind ?? "personal"` in its own constructor, so a decoded or constructed record always carries a string here and the ?? never evaluates its right side. The right operand's identical literal is killed, because `right` is the structural interface and may omit the kind.

ScopeRef's constructor is private and the only factory producing kind "project" is ScopeRef.project(tenantId, projectId), whose second parameter is a required ProjectId. A project scope therefore always carries a projectId, and this operand is constantly false wherever the kind test beside it is true. It is written so that store.loadProject(scope.projectId) typechecks against the optional field rather than needing an assertion, which is why the redundancy is deliberate: forcing it false is a runtime substitution the compiler never sees.

Control reaches this ternary only inside `if (scope.kind === "workspace")`, and both overloads of ScopeRef.workspace resolve a WorkspaceId before constructing — one through requireWorkspace, the other from the explicit third argument — so a workspace scope always carries one. Forcing the test false therefore always selects the loadWorkspace branch, which is the branch already taken. The test exists to narrow the optional field for that call; the undefined arm it guards would fail the canonicality check on the next line in any case.

nullableText has one consumer, decodeGrant's `(grant.attenuationOf?.value ?? null) !== nullableText(row, "parent_grant_id")`, and the null column has already returned on the line above. Removing the guard hands that comparison the raw column. Its left side is either null or a GrantId's value, which TextId forces to be a non-empty string, and the values this guard would have rejected are exactly the non-strings and the empty string — none of which is `===` to null or to a non-empty string. The comparison is therefore true wherever the guard would have thrown, and it throws corruptAuthority(), the identical error from the identical helper.

This mutant only lets the empty string through; every non-string still throws. An empty parent_grant_id then reaches decodeGrant's comparison against `grant.attenuationOf?.value ?? null`, whose two possible shapes are null and a GrantId value. GrantId extends TextId, which refuses an empty constructor argument, so neither shape can equal "" and the comparison is true. decodeGrant answers with corruptAuthority(), which is what nullableText would have thrown. The empty string is the only input separating the two forms and it produces the same refusal.

Forcing the left pair false leaves `value < 0`, so the accessor now returns any non-negative or non-numeric column. Every consumer compares the result against a field its record type pins to a non-negative safe integer: ScopeEpoch's constructor for epoch, Binding's for generation, and Revision's for the binding revision. A value that would have tripped this guard is either not a number, and so `!==` every number, or a number that is not a non-negative safe integer, and so `!==` every one that is. The enclosing disjunction is true and throws corruptAuthority(), the accessor's own error.

Because Number.isSafeInteger returns false for every non-Number, the conjunction this substitutes reduces to its left operand, and the guard becomes `typeof value !== "number" || value < 0`. It therefore admits fractional, unsafe and NaN columns it used to reject, and rejects nothing new. Each such column is then compared in loadSqliteEpoch, listSqliteEpochs or decodeBinding against an epoch, generation or revision that its record type has already forced to be a non-negative safe integer, so the comparison is unequal and corruptAuthority() is raised from the enclosing if instead of from here.

The whole condition forced false makes integer() a pass-through that returns the column untouched. Nothing downstream consumes it except four `!==` comparisons against record fields, and the record types behind them — ScopeEpoch's epoch, Binding's generation, and the Revision behind binding.revision — all refuse anything but a non-negative safe integer at construction, including on the decode path. Strict inequality against such a field is therefore true for every column this guard would have refused, and the surrounding if answers with the same corruptAuthority() instance shape.

Turning the final `||` into `&&` narrows the guard to columns that are both malformed and negative, so it throws on a strict subset of what it threw on before and never on anything new. On the difference — a non-number, a fractional number, or a non-negative unsafe one — the column flows out to the epoch, generation and revision comparisons, none of which can match a value outside the non-negative safe integers their record types enforce. Those comparisons raise corruptAuthority(), and no observation distinguishes which statement raised it.

This operand alone catches the negative safe integers, and forcing it false lets them through. A negative epoch column then meets `epoch.epoch !== integer(row, "epoch")`, and ScopeEpoch's constructor rejects a negative epoch, so the decoded record's epoch is non-negative and cannot equal it; the same holds for Binding's generation and for the Revision behind its revision column. Every negative column the guard would have refused is refused one line later, by the same corruptAuthority() the guard would have thrown.

Emptying the block leaves the condition evaluated and its result discarded, which is behaviourally the pass-through the whole-condition mutant produces. The four consumers each compare the returned column against a record field their type pins to a non-negative safe integer — ScopeEpoch's epoch, Binding's generation, and the Revision behind binding.revision — so a malformed column is unequal to it and the enclosing if throws corruptAuthority(). The refusal moves one statement later and keeps its code, message and class.

text() feeds two kinds of consumer here and both refuse a malformed column with corruptIdentity(). Most sites compare the result against a decoded record field — an id, a tenant id, a kind, a status, a canonical scope or subject key — every one of which is a non-empty string, so a non-string or empty column is unequal and the enclosing if throws. The rest wrap it in projectedId, whose TextId constructor refuses a non-string or empty argument and whose catch converts that TypeError into the very same corruptIdentity(). The mutant's only effect is which statement raises it.

With the length test forced false the accessor accepts an empty column and nothing else new. An empty id, kind, status, tenant id, role name, scope key or subject key then meets a comparison against the decoded record's own value, and none of those can be empty: TextId refuses an empty constructor argument, the kind and status unions have no empty member, and a canonical JSON key is never the empty string. Where the column instead feeds projectedId, TextId throws and projectedId's catch returns corruptIdentity() — the same error, from the same reader call.

The single consumer is loadWorkspace's `(workspace.projectId?.value ?? null) !== nullableText(row, "project_id")`, reached only after the explicit null column has returned above. The left side is null or a ProjectId value, which TextId forces to be a non-empty string. Every column this guard would refuse is a non-string or the empty string, neither of which is strictly equal to null or to a non-empty string, so the comparison is true and loadWorkspace throws corruptIdentity() — the error the guard would have thrown, one statement later.

This narrower mutant admits only the empty project_id column. loadWorkspace compares it against `workspace.projectId?.value ?? null`, which is null when the Workspace has no project and otherwise a ProjectId value — and ProjectId inherits TextId's refusal of an empty string, so it is never "". The comparison is therefore true, corruptIdentity() is thrown from loadWorkspace, and the only input that separates the mutant from the original produces the identical failure.

Reducing the guard to `value < 0` lets every non-numeric and every non-negative unsafe column through. Each of the six readers that call integer() does so as the last operand of its projection check, comparing the result against a Revision's value — the tenant's authorizationRevision, or the team, project, workspace, guest trust or membership revision. Revision's constructor admits only non-negative safe integers, so no such field equals a value this guard would have refused, and the reader throws corruptIdentity() exactly where the guard would have.

The conjunction collapses to its left operand, because a non-Number always makes Number.isSafeInteger false, so the guard becomes `typeof value !== "number" || value < 0` and now admits fractions, unsafe magnitudes and NaN. Those all reach a `revision.value !== integer(row, "revision")` comparison whose left side comes from a Revision, a class whose constructor rejects everything but a non-negative safe integer. Strict inequality holds, and the identity reader raises corruptIdentity() rather than the accessor.

With the whole condition false the accessor returns the revision column unchecked. It has exactly one shape of consumer in this file: a final disjunct comparing it against a decoded record's Revision value. Because Revision's constructor is the only way to build one and it refuses anything but a non-negative safe integer, and because every identity codec routes its revision through requireIdentityRevision into that constructor, the comparison is unequal for precisely the columns the guard rejected, and corruptIdentity() is raised from the enclosing if.

Requiring the column to be both malformed and negative shrinks the set the accessor refuses; it never grows it, because the mutated condition implies the original. On the shrunken difference the column travels to a revision comparison, and the Revision on the other side is a non-negative safe integer by construction, so the comparison is true and corruptIdentity() is thrown. Whether the tenant, team, project, workspace, guest trust or membership reader is running, its last projection operand is the one that fires.

Only the negative safe integers separate this mutant from the original. A negative revision column reaches a comparison against a Revision's value, and Revision refuses a negative argument outright — "Revision must be a non-negative safe integer" — so the decoded record cannot carry one to match it. The comparison is therefore true for every negative column the operand would have caught, and the reader answers with corruptIdentity(), the same error from the same load call.

An emptied block evaluates the condition and ignores it, so the accessor returns the raw revision column. That column is compared, in every one of the six readers that reads it, against a Revision value the record type has already constrained to the non-negative safe integers. Any column the block would have refused fails that comparison, and the reader throws corruptIdentity(). The observable difference is the stack frame the error is built in, which no assertion in this suite or any possible one inspects.

Every call to text() in this file sits inside decodeWatermark's projection check, comparing the column against the watermark key, the owner tenant id, the owner kind and id, or the holder's tenant and principal ids. Each of those is a non-empty string: TextId refuses empty ids, an ActorRef kind is a non-empty union member, and watermarkKey builds a canonical key. A column that is not a non-empty string is therefore unequal to it, and decodeWatermark throws corruptWatermark(), which is what text() would have thrown.

This mutant relaxes the guard only for the empty string. An empty watermark_key, owner_tenant_id, owner_kind, owner_id, holder_tenant_id or holder_principal_id column is then compared against the decoded watermark's corresponding value, and none of those values can be empty — the ids are TextIds, the owner kind is a non-empty literal, and watermarkKey never returns the empty string. The comparison is true, and decodeWatermark's own corruptWatermark() is raised in place of the accessor's.
